evidence_note: Standardised classification and segmentation tasks; common adaptation protocol and open benchmark, but no ecohydrological process target or explicit distribution-shift test.
Uniform testbed with three Sentinel-2 tasks and multiple label regimes; evaluation remains perception-centred and geographically narrow.

Eleven diverse dense-prediction datasets include biomass, burn scars and floods, multiple temporal configurations and broad geography, but most references are mapped products and physical or uncertainty diagnostics are absent.
Nineteen datasets add regression and temporal capability groups with a prescriptive protocol and repeated runs; explicit out-of-domain and physical-consistency tests are not the organising principle.
Standardised Landsat classification benchmarks and open resources test sensor-specific representation quality, not dynamic ecohydrological inference.

Twelve physically plausible image corruptions across six perception and vision-language tasks stress input robustness; adaptation differs by model family and no process or calibrated-uncertainty test is included.
Paired datasets test geography, time, scale, sensor and other real-world shifts under an open protocol; targets remain conventional EO tasks rather than coupled states or fluxes.

Four downstream tasks reveal task and cross-sensor dependence under end-to-end fine-tuning. This comparative study does not introduce a named benchmark or open common suite and does not test process consistency or uncertainty.
Five cryosphere segmentation datasets span sensors and regions and compare frozen, few-shot and fine-tuned settings; evaluation remains extent mapping rather than cryospheric process inference.

Region-disjoint crop segmentation and change detection reveal sharp transfer losses; shared-input conversion affects models differently and the labels do not directly observe crop water or carbon processes.

Five global environmental tasks include continuous soil properties, 12 modalities and random versus geographic splits; references are products or mapped labels and temporal and physical tests are limited.

Compares 11 runnable encoders and two served embedding products for biomass with geographic and temporal transfer; access modes differ and references are GEDI or mapped biomass products rather than flux observations.
Compares GFMs and task-specific baselines across three sensors, five-region holdouts and few-shot settings; inundation masks test event mapping but not flood hydraulics or calibrated uncertainty.
Yield, tillage and cover-crop tasks compare embeddings with purpose-built predictors across location, scale and time; results expose weak spatial transfer and time sensitivity.

ISMN station observations support spatial cross-validation of SAR, optical, meteorological and Prithvi features; temporal matching is tested, but no temporal holdout, water-balance check or uncertainty calibration is reported.

Gauge-based streamflow across 455 Australian catchments tests temporal and spatial generalisation against static descriptors; hydrological regimes are diagnosed but conservation and uncertainty are not explicitly benchmarked.

CAMELS-US gauge records and pseudo-ungauged folds support a factorial comparison of architecture and descriptor sets; NSE and latent diagnostics are reported without calibrated predictive uncertainty.
Held-out drought-season yield data test temporal distribution drift; the study shows that latent distance is not predictive uncertainty, but does not yet provide calibrated error estimates.

A retrospective field-season benchmark spans crops, climates, geography and time, tests early stress and yield-failure alerts and calibration, but prospective field efficacy and implementation release remain unestablished.

Identically trained sensor-specialist encoders are compared with AlphaEarth for hydrologic variables and unseen regions; sensor-variable alignment is physically interpretable, but reference directness and uncertainty remain limited.
